title: Integrated Geothermal Energy, Water Reuse, and Soilless Cultivation for Sustainable Greenhouse Vegetable Production in Arid Southern Tunisia: Enhancing Water and Energy Efficiency
content: Greenhouse vegetable production in the hyper-arid regions of southern Tunisia is constrained by water scarcity, large temperature fluctuations, rapid soil salinization, and the high economic and carbon costs of fossil-fuel heating. This study evaluates an integrated water–energy–food nexus model that combines (i) winter greenhouse heating with deep thermal groundwater from the Continental Intercalary (CI) aquifer, (ii) three-stage cascading reuse of cooled geothermal effluent, (iii) soilless substrate cultivation, and (iv) reverse osmosis (RO) desalination blended with raw geothermal water and disinfected drainage under sensor-driven fertigation. Sixteen deep boreholes (45–70 °C) yielded moderately to highly brackish waters (EC 3.42–5.40 dS m⁻¹; TDS 2.5–3.7 g L⁻¹; USSL classes C₄S₂–C₄S₃; SAR 4.95–9.78). Soils from 20 greenhouse perimeters were alkaline (pH 7.55–8.18) and strongly saline (ECe 5.35–28.47 dS m⁻¹). Compared with unheated soil-based production, the integrated geothermal soilless system raised marketable tomato yield from 8.5–12.0 to 24.5–32.0 kg m⁻² (+176%), reduced specific water consumption from 65–85 to 18–26 L kg⁻¹ (−70.5%), increased water-use efficiency (WUE) to 38.5–55.6 kg m⁻³, and extended the harvest window by five months (November–July versus March–June). Technical and socio-economic perspectives for smallholder adoption are outlined.
